channel.title: Palm Beach Coverage Blog
channel.description: Educational insurance guides and official resources for Palm Beach County.

item.title: Citizens Takeout Notices: How to Review Your Options
item.description: Read a Citizens depopulation notice using the actual offer deadline, coverage worksheets, and current official instructions.
item.content:encoded:
A Citizens depopulation notice requires attention to the actual offer form. Citizens says some offers make a policy ineligible to remain, and a policyholder who has a choice must register it by the date on the form. Do not assume a universal deadline from an online article. Citizens personal-lines instructions.

What to collect before deciding

Keep the complete packet, current declarations page, proposed coverage worksheets, and premium estimates together. Ask your agent to explain any item that is absent or unclear. Citizens provides comparison worksheets and estimated renewal premiums for available offers and the Citizens policy.

Create a simple comparison with a column for each offer. Record the insurer, policy form, limits, exclusions, deductibles, estimated premium, and proposed assumption or renewal date. Mark unknown entries as questions instead of filling them with assumptions.

Record your response

Use the response method specified in the official packet or work with your agent. Keep evidence of the submission and ask how to confirm the recorded choice. Contact information printed on a suspicious message should be checked against your existing policy documents or Citizens' official website.

Citizens' current instructions state there is no longer a 30-day post-assumption period to return to Citizens. Read the complete program instructions before relying on a right to reverse a transfer. Citizens policy assumption details.

A notice is specific to the policyholder

For an illustrative example, two neighbors might receive different offers and response dates. That is a hypothetical comparison, not a reported client case. Each person should use their own packet and obtain an explanation of their own eligibility.

Palm Beach Coverage does not process takeout responses or service insurance policies. This guide helps readers prepare questions for their current licensed agent.

item.title: Why Did My Florida Home Insurance Increase? Renewal Questions
item.description: Compare your old and new declarations pages and ask your insurer to explain changes in coverage, deductibles, discounts, and premium.
item.content:encoded:
If your renewal premium changed, start with the explanation for your own policy. A statewide average, a neighbor's premium, or a news headline cannot establish why your insurer changed your price. This guide replaces earlier unsupported market figures with a document-based review.

Put the documents side by side

Collect the prior declarations page, renewal declarations, endorsements, and any letter explaining the change. Write down the old and new amounts without assuming that the two policies have identical terms.

Ask your insurer or licensed agent to identify each changed item:

  • Did the insured limits or property information change?
  • Were any discounts added, removed, or recalculated?
  • Are the deductible amounts or their calculation different?
  • Did any coverage, exclusion, or endorsement change?
  • Is the payment schedule the same?
  • What part of the change is explained by the insurer's quoted rates?

Request an answer tied to the actual documents. Mark unanswered questions for follow-up rather than supplying a likely-sounding cause.

Compare an alternative carefully

Florida's consumer shopping guide discusses policy options and insurer-specific discount requirements. Use it to prepare questions; it does not provide a guaranteed saving for your property. Florida Insurance Consumer Advocate shopping guide.

Ask for the proposed terms in writing and confirm any conditions before treating another estimate as available replacement coverage. Keep the quote date and the professional's explanation with the comparison.

Keep the next step specific

For an illustrative scenario, a household might find that a limit changed at renewal and ask how that affected the premium. This is a hypothetical question, not a client case or a diagnosis of your renewal.

Palm Beach Coverage does not review policies for clients or sell insurance at this stage. Bring current insurance needs to a licensed professional. The publication and its waitlist are educational and prelaunch.

item.title: Florida SB 1028: Citizens Clearinghouse Status and Next Steps
item.description: Verified status of Florida SB 1028 and questions for Citizens commercial policyholders. Check your actual notice and current program instructions.
item.content:encoded:
SB 1028 became law in 2026. The Florida Senate record shows gubernatorial approval on June 16, 2026 and chapter number 2026-150. The final summary addresses Citizens eligibility and clearinghouse arrangements. Earlier drafts and summaries should not be treated as the final requirements. Official SB 1028 record and enacted text.

What changed in this guide

An earlier version described the bill as awaiting the Governor and presented specific implementation assumptions. This revision replaces those statements with the verified legislative status. It does not claim that every commercial policy will transfer on a single date.

Questions for a commercial policyholder

Start with the policy and correspondence for the business concerned. Ask the agent to identify the applicable program and explain any proposed change in writing.

  • Does this communication concern a new application, renewal, or assumption of an existing policy?
  • Which insurer would issue the replacement coverage?
  • Which limits, exclusions, deductibles, forms, and dates would change?
  • What action must the policyholder take, by what deadline, and how will receipt be confirmed?
  • Which provisions of the enacted law or current Citizens instructions support that answer?

Citizens maintains separate information for personal and commercial depopulation. Use the relevant program materials rather than applying a residential example to a commercial building. Citizens depopulation overview.

Keep the decision tied to the actual offer

Save the notice, comparison worksheet, written questions, and response confirmation together. Do not cancel existing insurance based solely on a blog summary. Have a licensed professional explain how the proposed dates relate to current coverage.

This page is an educational reading guide, not a legal opinion about an individual policy or a quotation from an insurer.

item.title: Florida HB 527 and AI Claim Denials: Verified Bill Status
item.description: HB 527 died in the Senate in March 2026. Understand the bill status and organize questions about an insurance claim decision.
item.content:encoded:
Florida's 2026 HB 527 proposed human-review requirements for certain insurance claim decisions involving artificial intelligence. The official record shows the bill died in Senate Rules on March 13, 2026. Its proposed effective date is not evidence that it became law. Official HB 527 record.

What this status does and does not tell you

The bill history establishes the outcome of this specific proposal. It does not establish that an insurer can lawfully deny any claim, that every automated process is unlawful, or that other statutes and policy duties do not apply. This page makes no conclusion about whether an individual denial complied with the law.

Questions to organize after a denial

Use the insurer's written decision and your own policy as the starting point. Ask for a clear explanation of the policy provisions and facts relied upon. If you are concerned about automated processing, ask what review occurred and how to request clarification.

Keep the following together:

  • The decision letter and date received.
  • The applicable policy and endorsements.
  • The documents submitted with the claim.
  • Your written questions and any response.
  • Any stated review or response deadlines.

Do not infer the use of AI merely from a fast or unsatisfactory response. A disputed decision and proof of automated decision-making are different factual questions.

When the dispute needs individual advice

For a dispute about legal rights, deadlines, or remedies, seek a qualified professional who can review the actual documents. This publication does not handle claims, investigate insurers, or give legal representation.

Earlier broad statements about the absence of all legal protections have been removed because the fate of one bill cannot support that conclusion.

item.title: Florida Roof Age and HB 815: Corrected Bill Status
item.description: HB 815 died in March 2026. Read the corrected status, existing statutory roof provisions, and questions to ask about an inspection or renewal.
item.content:encoded:
Florida HB 815 did not become law in the 2026 session. The official record says it died in the House Insurance & Banking Subcommittee on March 13, 2026. The July 1 date printed on the proposed bill was not an enacted effective date. Official HB 815 record.

Correction to the earlier article

The earlier title and summary implied that HB 815 created new protections taking effect in July. That was incorrect. This revision removes the unsupported change-in-law claim, roof price tables, savings forecasts, and unverified first-person client anecdotes.

Existing law is a separate question

The published 2025 edition of section 627.7011 contains existing homeowners-policy roof-age provisions. It restricts age-only refusals for roofs under 15 years and provides an inspection pathway for older roofs where an authorized inspection establishes at least five years of useful life. The section also states limits on its application and preserves other lawful underwriting grounds. Read the whole section and check current applicability with a qualified professional. Florida Statutes section 627.7011.

What to ask your insurer

  • What is the written reason for the inspection or replacement request?
  • Which policy and legal requirements are being applied?
  • Who is acceptable to perform the inspection?
  • What documentation is needed, and by what date?
  • How will the insurer acknowledge receipt and communicate its decision?

Keep permit records, prior inspection reports, photographs, and correspondence together. Do not assume that a roof's birthday alone guarantees either approval or denial.

This guide does not determine your legal rights, an insurer's underwriting decision, or whether a particular roof needs replacement. Ask a licensed professional to review the actual documents; Palm Beach Coverage does not provide those services.

item.title: Palm Beach County Hurricane Planning and Insurance Checklist
item.description: Organize policy records, emergency contacts, and a household plan using official Florida preparedness resources.
item.content:encoded:
Prepare the household plan alongside the insurance paperwork. Florida's Division of Emergency Management recommends an emergency plan and stocked supplies, and directs residents to their county emergency-management program for current local information. Florida Plan & Prepare resources.

Organize the documents

Save copies of declarations pages, policy endorsements, insurer contacts, and a record of important belongings where you can reach them if you leave home. Record questions that need an insurer's response, rather than assuming a document means a specific loss is covered.

Ask the policy questions early

  • Which policy covers the risks you are discussing?
  • What exclusions and deductibles apply?
  • When would a requested change actually become effective?
  • How should a loss be reported, and what information should be retained?
  • Who should be contacted if online access is unavailable?

Do not assume that coverage can be bought or changed immediately as a storm approaches. Confirm timing with the insurer; this guide does not state a universal binding restriction or deadline.

Make the practical plan

Use the official preparedness links to review supplies, evacuation planning, and support for household members who may need assistance. Follow current instructions from local emergency officials rather than an old blog date.

Write down who will contact whom, how household members will reconnect, and where essential records will be stored. Review the plan with the people who will use it. Include pets and any accessibility needs in the discussion.

After the immediate danger

Follow official safety instructions. Use the claims contact listed in the policy and ask the insurer what records it needs. This publication does not replace emergency instructions, inspect damage, or handle claims.

Palm Beach Coverage is a prelaunch project; the checklist is educational and does not establish insurance coverage.

item.title: My Safe Florida Home: Official Program and Application Guide
item.description: Find official My Safe Florida Home inspection and grant instructions. Check current eligibility and approval before assuming funding.
item.content:encoded:
My Safe Florida Home provides wind-mitigation inspections and grant assistance for approved improvements. Its official site describes an inspection process followed by a grant application for eligible homes. Program participation and funding should be checked through the official instructions, not assumed from a blog headline. My Safe Florida Home program.

Start with the official program

Open the current program site and its participant resources. Review the eligibility questions and required steps before arranging work. Keep the current instructions with your application records so you can distinguish what was requested from what was approved.

Ask the program these questions if the answers are unclear:

  • Which inspection and grant requirements apply to this property?
  • What documents must be supplied?
  • Which improvements are eligible for this application?
  • What approval is required before work begins?
  • What costs are the homeowner's responsibility?
  • What records and deadlines apply to reimbursement?

Treat the inspection as information

Read the report and ask about recommended improvements. Obtain clear written scopes for any work being considered. A suggested improvement, a submitted application, and an approved grant are different steps; do not treat them as interchangeable.

The program also encourages owners to share completed improvements with their insurer to discuss available discounts. This article does not promise an award amount, a premium reduction, or a project payback period. Official program guidance.

Keep proof of each step

Save applications, approval notices, inspection reports, contracts, invoices, and submitted documents together. Use the program's official support channels for a question about an individual application.

Palm Beach Coverage is an independent educational publication, not the grant administrator, an approved contractor, or an operating insurance agency. This revision removes earlier unsupported cost and savings examples and does not report a client result.

item.title: Florida Homeowners Insurance: A Practical Renewal Review
item.description: Review a Florida homeowners renewal using policy terms and written quotes, without unsupported statewide averages or promised savings.
item.content:encoded:
A useful insurance review starts with the cost and coverage offered to your household. A statewide average cannot tell you whether your renewal is suitable. This guide replaces earlier unsupported premium statistics and savings promises with a practical comparison process.

Compare what is actually offered

The Florida Insurance Consumer Advocate recommends understanding policy options, discounts, deductibles, and replacement-cost versus actual-cash-value terms. Discount requirements differ among insurers. Florida consumer shopping guidance.

Gather your current declarations page, renewal notice, and any alternative written quotes. Label each quote with its date. Ask which quoted terms remain subject to inspection or underwriting before treating an estimate as an available policy.

Make a comparison you can explain

For each offer, record the total quoted premium, coverage limits, deductible amounts, exclusions, and policy form. Leave a question mark where documentation is missing. Ask a licensed professional to explain the differences in language you can use yourself.

Consider the cost you would need to meet after a covered loss as well as the payment due now. Do not choose a larger deductible solely because a headline promises a certain discount.

Keep savings claims specific

A bundle or improvement may be worth asking about, but this publication does not promise a percentage reduction, a particular premium, or a carrier placement. Compare actual offers for your circumstances.

For an illustrative scenario, a lower-premium quote could also have a different deductible. That hypothetical example is a prompt to compare terms, not a reported client result.

Know who is providing the service

Palm Beach Coverage currently publishes education and collects interest in future launch updates. It does not quote, place, renew, or service insurance. Use your current licensed professional for an immediate policy decision.

item.title: Flood Insurance in Palm Beach County: Questions to Ask
item.description: A practical guide to reviewing flood policy terms, building and contents protection, exclusions, and start dates with official FEMA resources.
item.content:encoded:
Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program offers flood policies for homeowners, renters, and businesses. Building and contents coverage have distinct terms and deductibles. FEMA flood policy guide.

Read the proposed coverage

Bring a description of the property and the belongings you want to discuss. Ask a licensed professional to identify the applicable form and explain the proposed policy in writing.

  • Does the proposal address the building, belongings, or both?
  • What limits and deductibles apply to each part?
  • Which exclusions matter for the way you use the property?
  • When would coverage start, and what conditions must be met first?
  • Who handles policy changes, renewals, and claims?

Avoid treating every kind of water damage as the same insured event. Ask the insurer how the cause of a loss affects the coverage being discussed.

Compare documents, not labels

If comparing an NFIP proposal with a private flood proposal, request the actual coverage documents for each. A name or premium alone does not tell you whether the proposals meet the same needs. This guide does not promise that either option is available, cheaper, or more suitable for a particular address.

Prepare a useful record

Keep the quote date, quoted terms, source documents, and the professional's written answers together. Recheck the details before purchasing rather than relying on an earlier estimate.

This revision removes unsupported local premium statistics and reported client experiences from the earlier article. No Palm Beach Coverage customer result is claimed. For an immediate flood-insurance question, contact a licensed professional; this publication is still a prelaunch project.

item.title: Florida Hurricane Deductibles: Read Your Policy First
item.description: Locate your hurricane deductible, check the trigger and dollar exposure, and use Florida DFS guidance on calendar-year rules.
item.content:encoded:
Find the hurricane deductible on your policy's declarations page and ask your insurer to explain it. Florida DFS distinguishes hurricane coverage from flood coverage and describes calendar-year deductible rules when coverage stays with the same insurer or insurer group. Surplus-lines policies may differ. Florida DFS hurricane deductible guide.

Confirm the trigger

Do not use the phrase named storm as a substitute for the actual hurricane definition and policy terms. Ask which deductible would apply to the event being discussed and how the insurer determined that result.

Put the policy's amount into dollars

If your declarations show a percentage, ask what insured amount it applies to and whether endorsements change that amount. Have the insurer confirm the resulting dollar exposure. This guide does not assume that all homeowners policies offer the same deductible choices.

For an illustrative arithmetic example only, two percent of $300,000 is $6,000. Those numbers are invented for the calculation; they are not a quote, recommended limit, or statement about any client's coverage.

Ask about more than one loss

Keep claim records and ask the insurer how any earlier loss is credited under the applicable calendar-year provisions. Do not assume a second storm always has no deductible or that a credit transfers to a different insurance company.

Keep the explanation with your records

Save the declarations, relevant endorsements, written explanation, and claim references together. If the terms are unclear, consult the insurer or a licensed professional before relying on a projected payment.

Palm Beach Coverage is a prelaunch educational project. This page does not calculate an insurer's settlement or provide claim-handling services.
